No telemetry and no vendor account is a rare pitch for a Git client, most of them quietly assume you'll sign in somewhere. The thing I'd actually test on day one with self-hosted GitLab is a custom CA, a lot of enterprise instances sit behind TLS interception or an internal proxy. Does BeeBranch read the OS trust store for that, or do you need to feed it a cert yourself?

@galdayan

Thanks — no telemetry, no vendor account, and nothing leaves the machine unless you explicitly connect a forge. Self-hosted is the primary target, so the instance URL must be https and verification is never disabled — there's no "ignore certificates" switch. [...] Honest answer on your day-one test: there are two TLS layers. The GitLab/GitHub API client is rustls with a pinned root set — today it does not read the OS trust store. For an internal CA you paste the PEM once per instance; it's stored locally (SQLite) and added as an extra root, alongside the pinned ones.

Clone/fetch/push are delegated to your own git, so that path uses Git's TLS stack and the OS store, and we passthrough SSL_CERT_FILE, SSL_CERT_DIR, CURL_CA_BUNDLE and the standard proxy variables. The imported instance PEM is not injected into Git yet — that's a known gap for TLS-interception setups.

results.title: Timestream: A Local-First Git Client Built Around the Commit Graph | Indie Chains
results.content:
Timestream is a desktop Git client that makes the repository timeline the main surface, then puts review, commit, SSH, and GitHub actions around it. The product is intentionally opinionated: give the working tree a desk, make the next state visible, and keep the local repository in the driver's seat.

Timestream presents the working tree, split diff, and filing context as one visual review desk.

## The commit graph as the starting point

The product's central idea is simple: history should be read as a graph, not only as a list of messages. Timestream places the default branch down the centre of the view and lets other branches fork away as spurs. Selecting a commit gives the developer a concrete place to inspect what changed. [...] Authentication can use a GitHub App device flow or a personal access token. The result is a focused bridge between a local branch and the collaborative review surface where a team can discuss and merge it.

## A focused desktop workflow

The product's path can be understood as four deliberate moves. Each one answers a different question, and together they keep the workflow close to the repository instead of spreading it across a command line, a diff viewer, and multiple browser tabs. [...] The current v0.1 release is positioned for Windows, macOS, and Linux AppImage. It is also open source under AGPL-3.0, which gives technically minded users a clear path to inspect the project and follow its future releases.

## Why Indie Chains recommends Timestream

Indie Chains editorial

Timestream has a clear product thesis: make Git history feel readable, then keep the actions around that history close enough to stay in flow. The visual timeline gives the product a memorable point of view, while the review desk and push guardrails make that point of view practical.
